To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a major contributor to insulin resistance in the liver.
HCV induces insulin resistance in hepatocytes through the induction of PGC-1alpha, which is a master regulator of hepatic metabolism.
PGC-1a is a critical regulator of HCV infection and that HCV infection induces PGC-1b expression in the liver, leading to hepatic insulin insensitivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of PPARγ coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) in the regulation of glucose homeostasis, insulin sensitivity and hepatic steatosis in mice and humans.
the role of the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1alpha in the pathogenesis of HCV-induced insulin resistance.
the effects of hepatitis C virus infection on the development of insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis in the liver.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hepatitis C virus infection causes insulin resistance, but that the mechanisms by which the virus causes insulin resistance remain to be elucidated.
HCV infection causes insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, but this relationship is not as simple as it may seem.
the hepatitis C virus infection is a risk factor for the development of diabetes mellitus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PGC-1a/AMPK pathway is a key regulator of hepatic glucose metabolism.
the metabolic regulator PGC1alpha is a crucial mediator of hepatic insulin resistance and steatosis in the setting of chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.
PGC-1alpha links hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection with insulin resistance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is linked to hepatic insulin insensitivity.
the hepatitis C virus (HCV) can directly cause insulin resistance in the liver.
the metabolic regulator PGC1alpha links hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection to hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance.
